newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK leader Tung - master or prisoner in own house?.
newsitem.headline: HK leader Tung - master or prisoner in own house?.

text.p: When billionaire shipping magnate Tung Chee-hwa was overwhelmingly selected as Hong Kong's first post-colonial leader, he declared with satisfaction: Now we are masters in our own house.
But Tung, 60, groomed from boyhood to take over as unquestioned patriarch of the family business empire, is already presiding over an increasingly unruly household.

Hong Kong's populist democratic lobby has dismissed him as China's puppet. They are waging a public opinion war at home and abroad against his policies which they argue will snuff out the freedoms that made Hong Kong so successful.
He has to contend with Beijing's ageing leaders hovering in the background like over-anxious parents second-guessing his every move, diplomats say.

On the one hand Beijing fears Hong Kong's pro-democracy forces may infect China itself. On the other, it is desperate to ensure that Hong Kong, so successful under 156 years of British colonial rule, will not fall to pieces under China.

And to add insult to injury, Hong Kong's first home-bred leader finds himself less popular than outgoing British Governor Chris Patten, an appointee from a distant capital who doesn't speak Chinese, a Baptist University public poll showed in June.
The Hong Kong of 1997 is a very different place from the docile colony with its rubber-stamp appointed legislature in place when Britain and China sealed its fate in 1984.
In the 13 years since the handover treaty was signed, a new generation has come of age.
Most are the sons and daughters of refugees who fled China and have grown up to become members of Hong Kong's well- educated, prosperous and confident middle class.
But they don't share their parents' refugee mentality which regards Hong Kong as a temporary stopover, a waiting room to the West or one day back to China.
They consider themselves Hong Kong people. They want a say in governing their own lives.
China's military crackdown on the youthful protesters around Tiananmen Square on June 4, 1989 was the watershed for many of Hong Kong's six million people.

One million took to the streets in horror at the brutality of their future rulers, smashing a myth that Hong Kong was an apolitical community interested only in accumulating hard cash, said Michael DeGolyer, director of the long-term 1997 Transition Project at Baptist University.

Out of the bloodshed to the north grew Hong Kong's pro-democracy movement -- and Hong Kong's most popular party, the Democratic Party led by lawyer Martin Lee, a critic of both colonialism and Beijing-style authoritarianism.
It catapulted a younger generation of self-assured young politicians to the forefront.

Christine Loh, 41, a lawyer-businesswoman, epitomises the new class of young Hong Kong legislators. An ardent advocate of democracy, of universal adult suffrage and environmental responsibility she will be swept out of office at the June 30 handover.

Angered by mild democratic reforms introduced as more than 150 years of colonial rule drew to a close, China will dismantle the Legislative Council and replace it with a selected interim Provisional Legislature expected to serve for about a year.
The Democracy Party, pro-democracy independents and the smaller democracy parties which refused to cooperate with Beijing's selection process will share Loh's fate.
They have no intention of withdrawing gracefully. They aim to challenge the constitutional legality of the interim chamber.
"Keep my seat warm," yelled the Democratic Party's Lee during a demonstration against the Provisional Legislature staged as 1996 gave way to 1997.

Loh, an independent legislator, has responded by founding a new party, the Citizens' Party, to push for more democracy and to contest elections scheduled for 1998 -- under new electoral laws that will reverse the British reforms.
"For those of us who are relatively young, to be able to say we've gone through the process of getting the people's mandate, it's a big deal," she said in a recent intererview.
"It might not be a big deal in the West, but for us it's a big deal."
Tung cites as his political mentors Singapore's elder stateman Lee Kuan Yew, "iron lady" Margaret Thatcher and China's late hardline paramount leader Deng Xiaoping.
He argues Hong Kong needs to give up some civil liberties -- accept police vetting of political demonstrations and outlaw foreign donations--to safeguard stability.
Christine Loh's generation has little time for Tung's paternalistic approach and emphasis on "Asian values".
